name: Old Persian
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: We do not know the rules for Old Persian stress, but some rules may be formulated from comparison with other Iranian languages and Indic. In words of two, three, or four syllables, the heavy syllable closest to the end of the word, not counting the last syllable, probably took the stress. Here "heavy syllable" = a syllable with a long vowel or a diphthong or a short vowel followed by more than one consonant (or an unwritten n or h + cons.) and "light syllable" = syllable with a short vowel followed by only one consonant: kā´ra, Višt´āspa, ām´ātā, Auramazd´āha, kāsakáina / vaz´ạrka, Auramázdā, Ariyārámna / fr´ābara, duvit´āparanam / mártiya, víspazanā [...] In words with several short syllables the stress moved toward the beginning of the word: bága, návama, but we do not know how far it was allowed to go
new_statements.citation: Skjærvø, Prods Oktor. 2016. An Introduction to Old Persian (Old Persian Primer 2016). Harvard University course text.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Reconstructed, not attested: stress on the rightmost heavy (long-vowel, diphthong, or closed) non-final syllable; if there is none, stress retracts toward the beginning of the word (how far is unknown). Final syllables are excluded except possibly closed finals (undecidable). A later drift to fixed penultimate stress is 'possible, even probable' on Middle Persian evidence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only in a conjectural example: 'hamáranakàra (à = secondary stress)' as one of several possible stressings of a five-short-syllable word; no rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: Author states the rules are unknown; whether closed final syllables could bear stress (Kúrauš vs Kuráuš) is undecidable; position in words with epenthetic vowels (xšāyaθiya < *xšāyaθya, Haxāmanišiya, θanuvaniya) is 'a matter of conjecture'; whether stress shifted in genitive-dative forms (kārahạya) is unknown; possible generalization of penult stress during the OP period (naváma > *nowóm). Kent 1950 §59(i) p. 25 and Meillet-Benveniste 1931 §173 p. 101 both say explicitly that the inscriptions give no evidence of the accent's position (Kent: only that enclitics show 'there was an accent'). Meillet-Benveniste 1931 §103 p. 63 separately infers initial stress in the trisyllable xšāyaθ(i)ya from šāh, 'car l'accent ne remonte pas au delà de l'antépénultième'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms of nouns, names, verbs in a teaching grammar). The language is extinct and the script marks no accent; every statement is a comparative reconstruction from Indic, other Iranian, and Middle/New Persian outcomes, not an observation. The pedagogical grammar itself is marked 'do not cite in print without the author's permission'.
new_statements.identity_note: Old Persian proper (oldp1255), the language of the Achaemenid royal inscriptions; extinct, script unaccented. Skjærvø's rule covers Old Persian as a whole; Meillet-Benveniste note that xšāyaθiya is a Median loan. Not to be confused with Middle Persian (pahl1241) or the Old Persian language subgroup node oldp1254.

In words of two, three, or four syllables, the heavy syllable closest to the end of the word, not counting the last syllable, probably took the stress. sources.note: 'We do not know the rules for Old Persian stress'; by comparison with other Iranian and Indic it proposes that in words of 2-4 syllables the heavy syllable closest to the end, not counting the last, probably took the stress (kā´ra, Auramázdā, mártiya); in words of several short syllables stress moved toward the beginning (bága, návama) but how far is unknown; final closed syllables of unknown status; a later shift to the penult is 'possible, even probable' on Middle Persian evidence; stress of xšāyaθiya etc. 'a matter of conjecture'.

sources.note: 'There is no evidence as to the position and nature of the syllabic accent of OP, except that the presence of enclitic words shows that there was an accent.' (archive.org 'oldpers'; a second archive.org copy, /, is the same 1950 printing with identical text).

sources.citation: Meillet, Antoine. 1931. Grammaire du vieux-perse. 2e éd. entièrement corrigée et augmentée par Émile Benveniste. Paris: Champion. §173, p. 101 and §103, p. 63.
sources.note: §173 (p. 101): the Persian inscriptions, like the Avesta and all ancient IE inscriptions, contain nothing that informs either on a possible preservation of the Indo-Iranian tone or on the place of an accent; the Indo-Iranian quantitative rhythm surely existed in Persian, but whether a mobile tone survived or had become fixed cannot be said. §103 (p. 63), in an etymological argument: the outcome šāh < xšāyaθiya 'indique un trisyllabe accentué sur l'initiale xšāyaθ(i)ya, car l'accent ne remonte pas au delà de l'antépénultième'.

sources.citation: Meillet, Antoine. 1915. Grammaire du vieux perse. Paris: Guilmoto. §173 (PDF p. 115).
sources.note: Same statement as the 1931 §173: nothing in the inscriptions informs on the Indo-Iranian tone or on the place of an accent; quantitative rhythm surely existed; impossible to say whether traces of a mobile tone (as in Vedic) survived.
